fixes.explanation: Not this time, friend. The writer says it's pleasing when you keep the words “…within you and they are constantly on your lips.” That's inside you and out loud, both together. So the statement is true just as written.

The gate is in the very next verse, so I see why that one tempted you. But this verse says you'll “…soundly answer those who sent you?” The elders aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage. The gate there is where the writer warns against crushing the afflicted, and that's a different saying.

Right on the money. The writer says, “…or you may learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.” Notice the word "may." The danger he names is picking up the angry man's ways. I've picked up a few habits from the junk drawer myself, and I'm still shaking some of them.

Debts do come up soon, but in a different saying. For the hot-tempered man, the writer says, “…or you may learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.” The reason is you learning his ways. Pledges and security for debts show up a couple of verses later.

Prophets don't show up in this saying. The verse says the skilled man “…will be stationed in the presence of kings; he will not stand before obscure men.” Kings are the answer, and obscure men are the other side of the picture. Prophets are good company, but this verse didn't send them an invitation.

That's it. The writer says, “Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive.” He doesn't spell out how it deceives, and I won't make that up for him. The warning is plain: delicacies on a ruler's table, and the writer still says don't crave them.

The verse never says that. It says, “Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive.” Servants aren't in this saying at all. Even the fanciest food on a ruler's table gets a warning label here, and I'd read it.

Nothing in the verse mentions saving anything for later. The writer says, “Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive.” The reason given is that the food is deceptive, not that it's being set aside. He doesn't say how it deceives, so I'll leave that open.

The picture goes the other way, friend. The writer says, “When you glance at wealth, it disappears…” The wealth makes wings and flies off, so it isn't something that stays with whoever goes after it. That's why the verse before says to “be wise enough to restrain yourself.”

That's not what the text says is going on inside him. The writer says, “…he is keeping track, inwardly counting the cost.” His heart, the verse says, “…is not with you.” Staying all night isn't mentioned anywhere, but counting the cost is.

Priests aren't named in this verse. The writer says, “Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless…” The warning covers two things: moving the stone and encroaching on those fields. The fatherless are the ones whose fields are named, and the next verse adds, “…for their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you.”
